summary: Describes an EPP mapping for provisioning and managing contacts, individual or organizational identifiers, in a shared central repository. It obsoletes RFC 3733. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 5733.

plainLanguage.summary: A registry keeps a list of the people and companies who own names. This note says how to add or change them using EPP.

subtitle: Managing individual and organizational contacts in domain registries

tldr.problem: Domain registry systems need a standard way to store and manage contact information for individuals and organizations. Without standardization, each registry implements contacts differently, making integration difficult.
tldr.mechanism: EPP Contact Mapping defines XML-based commands (check, info, create, delete, update, transfer) that allow registrars to manage contact objects in shared central repositories, with support for multiple languages and data disclosure controls.
tldr.outcome: Registries can now use uniform contact management across EPP. This RFC replaced RFC 3733 and was itself replaced by RFC 5733 with minor clarifications.

facts.label: Address fields
facts.value: Street (1-3 optional), City, State/Province (optional), Postal Code (optional), Country Code

facts.label: Contact status values
facts.value: ok, linked, client*/server* prefixed (Delete, Transfer, Update, Create), pending*

facts.value: ITU E.164: +[country code].[number] with optional extension

today: RFC 4933 was a Draft Standard published in May 2007 and has been obsoleted by RFC 5733. The obsoleting RFC incorporated minor clarifications and corrections based on implementation experience but the core contact mapping concepts remain the same. It is an update to RFC 3733.

sections.title: Introduction to EPP Contact Mapping
sections.content:
EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) is a framework for managing provisioning of domain names and related objects. The EPP Contact Mapping defines how contact objects—representing individuals or organizations—are stored, queried, and managed within a shared central repository using XML syntax.

A contact object contains social information identifiers such as names, addresses, telephone numbers, and email addresses. Organizations use contacts to identify the various parties involved in domain registrations (registrants, administrative contacts, technical contacts, etc.). This mapping builds on the base EPP specification and applies its command and response structures to contact-specific operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact is like an address card in a registry database. It holds someone's name, address, phone, and email. EPP Contact says how to add, find, and update these cards so everyone follows the same rules.

sections.title: Contact Attributes and Status
sections.content:
Each contact object has a unique server identifier and a Repository Object Identifier (ROID) assigned at creation. Contacts carry mandatory and optional attributes: name and org (both internationalized and localized forms), address (street, city, state/province, postal code, country code per ISO 3166), voice and fax telephone numbers following ITU E.164 format, and email address.

Every contact has a status field that controls operations and visibility. Status values include ok (normal state), clientDeleteProhibited and serverDeleteProhibited (prevent deletion), linked (associated with other objects like domains), and pendingCreate, pendingDelete, pendingTransfer, pendingUpdate (actions awaiting completion). The disclose element allows clients to specify which attributes should be withheld from public disclosure based on the registry's data collection policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Contacts have personal details like name, address, and email. Each contact can have status labels like 'locked' or 'waiting for approval' that control what you can do with it. Some info can be hidden from the public.

sections.title: Query Commands: Check, Info, and Transfer Status
sections.content:
EPP defines three query commands for retrieving contact information. The <check> command tests whether one or more contact identifiers can be provisioned (are available) without committing to creation. The server responds with availability status and optional reason text for each identifier.

The <info> command retrieves detailed information about a specific contact including all attributes, status values, creation and modification dates, transfer history, and authorization information. The querying client only receives authorization information if they are the sponsoring client.

The <transfer> query operation retrieves the status of a pending or completed contact transfer request, including who requested it, when, and when the receiving client must respond.
sections.plainLanguage: Query commands are like asking a librarian 'Do you have contact sh8013?', 'Tell me everything about it', or 'What's the status of transferring it to another registrar?'

sections.title: Transform Commands: Create, Delete, Update, and Transfer
sections.content:
Transform commands modify contact state. The <create> command provisions a new contact object by specifying the desired identifier, postal information (in one or two formats), contact details, an authorization password, and optional disclosure preferences. The server returns the created identifier and creation timestamp.

The <delete> command removes a contact from the repository. Servers typically reject deletion if the contact is linked to other objects (like domains). The <update> command modifies contact attributes through add/remove/change operations on status, postal information, telephone numbers, email, authorization info, and disclosure settings.

The <transfer> command manages contact sponsorship changes between clients, supporting request, approve, reject, and cancel operations. Transform commands may be processed immediately or deferred (status code 1001) pending offline human review, in which case the contact status becomes pendingCreate, pendingUpdate, etc., and clients are later notified of completion.
sections.plainLanguage: Transform commands are like telling the librarian 'Create a new contact', 'Delete this one', 'Change the phone number', or 'Transfer it to another registrar'. Some changes might need approval first.

sections.title: Internationalization and Technical Considerations
sections.content:
Contact mappings support both internationalized (7-bit ASCII-safe UTF-8) and localized (unrestricted UTF-8) forms for names, organizations, and addresses. This allows registries to serve global clients while accommodating local scripts. All dates and times use UTC in XML Schema format (e.g., '1999-04-03T22:00:00.0Z').

The specification leverages XML and XML Schema for formal syntax validation. Authorization information protects transfer operations and information queries; both client and server MUST protect this data with encryption. Contact object ROID identifiers remain stable for the object's lifetime and are used in internal registry operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Contacts can have names and addresses in any language, but they're all stored in a standard format with dates in UTC. Authorization passwords keep transfers secure.
